I don't own the game, Ive just been watching a lot of youtube videos about it. I am very interested in procedurally generated worlds but what I like about them is that it can generate something that nobody else has seen. The best example I can find of that is Dwarf Fortress and all the crazy stories people have shared about things they have found in their generated world. Even though the game uses basic building blocks to make the world, its complicated enough to come up with some amazingly varied things.

From what Ive seen of NMS, all the creatures and plants look like they draw from a fairly limited pool of 'pieces' to build the animals. I've watched a few streamers/youtubers and even though they all started in different parts of the games universe, the creatures they find look very similar. I only had to watch a few before I saw the same things walking around.

With billions of randomly generated planets, do you think theres is anything out there worth exploring for? Maybe some chance combination of terrain, flora and fauna that makes a planet look truly unique compared to all the others we have seen? Even googling "weirdest No Mans Sky discoveries" just comes up with pictures of things Ive seen 10 times already in various videos.

I was interested in the game before it came out. I knew it wouldnt live up to the hype but the idea of exploring space to find something nobody has seen before appeals to me... but after watching some gameplay I'm not sure if the game has the ability to generate anything truly interesting.
No Mans Sky - Do you think there are any amazing/unique discoveries to be made among the billions of planets?

The game was purely run on the hype train. Now lo and behold, the hype train has crashed miserably, as per usual.

As for the Dwarf Fortress thingie - this might be a unique example for a randomly generated game because DF has an absolutely obscene amount of variables (and the occasional bug) that can result in all sorts of shenanigans. It also heavily builds on the player's own imagination, as the ASCII graphics don't tell much of a story on their own, and the behavior of the various entities within the game are, when seen without the classical DF romanticism, fairly simple routines.

No Man's Sky, on the other hand, is all about the visuals, but only has a so many art assets - which does not work out with the millions of different planets to explore that the developers promised.
